name: Fort Nassau
label: Fort Nassau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort Nassau' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/365223149: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Nassau' (52 m across).
notes: Hilltop fort with a panoramic view over the harbour and city.

text.description: Fort Nassau sits on top of a hill above Willemstad, and that height is what makes it worth a stop with a phone. From the terrace you look out over St. Anna Bay, the arched Queen Juliana Bridge and the rooftops of Punda and Otrobanda below. The fort was built in the 1790s, finished in late 1797, and it is a rectangular battery inside a ring wall. It has had three names: Fort Republiek, then Fort George under British rule from 1807, and Fort Oranje Nassau from 1816, which most people shorten to Fort Nassau. It later served as a control tower for the Queen Emma Bridge, and since 1959 it has been a restaurant. The hill is about 68 metres high, so the view carries a long way across the harbour. The best picture here is the bay, with the fort's terrace in the foreground to give the scene depth. The far west end of the restaurant terrace is the spot to aim for. One guide calls it the best place for photos of St. Anna Bay, and it is usually calmer than the busy sunset corner. You can walk around the top of the fort, but not into the harbour control area. If you turn north, the refinery comes into view, which some visitors find less pleasing, so keep your frame towards the bay.
text.geographic_location: Fort Nassau stands on a hill overlooking Willemstad and its harbour, with Punda and Otrobanda visible below.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram, station or other public transport information is available for this spot. The approach road is steep and a little confusing, and people jog along it, so take care. Parking is to the right of the entrance. Once there, go to the far west end of the terrace. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bay and the bridge with the terrace in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the harbour and the city in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the arch of the Queen Juliana Bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look over St. Anna Bay and the arched Queen Juliana Bridge, with the fort's terrace in the foreground. If you want the walls and terrace against a sunset sky over the harbour, the sunset corner is the alternative, though it is more crowded.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Include a piece of the terrace, such as the edge or a wall, in the bottom of the frame so the view has a foreground. Keep the bridge arch off-centre and avoid pointing north towards the refinery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the water to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Wipe the lens first, as terrace air can be salty and leave a haze on the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset gives warm light over the harbour, but the terrace is busier then, and the restaurant advises booking for sunset. A morning visit is quieter.

text.access_note: Entry to the fort may be free, but the restaurant is paid and reservations are advised, so check the official site before you go for current opening hours.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon and sunset light is warm and flattering over the harbour.
The terrace is likely to be quieter in the morning than at sunset.
Sea air can leave a salty haze on a phone lens, so wiping it first helps.
Facing north from the terrace points towards the refinery, which may spoil the view.

name: Fort Amsterdam
label: Fort Amsterdam
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort Amsterdam' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3190150018: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fort Amsterdam'.
notes: 17th-century fort housing the governor's palace and the Fort Church.

text.description:
Fort Amsterdam stands at the mouth of St. Anna Bay, right beside the harbour in the heart of Willemstad. The fort was built in 1634, and the city of Willemstad grew up outside its walls. It still has a working role: the offices of Curaçao's government and governor are inside. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the colour. The ochre and yellow walls look bright against the sky and the water, and the courtyard gives you a good close view of the fort's buildings and its church.

The Dutch West India Company built the fort as a military base and as its headquarters. Its walls are about three metres thick. Look at the south-western wall of the Fort Church and you can find a cannonball from 1804, left there when a British naval captain attacked the fort. The fort is now part of the UNESCO World Heritage area of Willemstad's inner city and harbour.

Start in the courtyard for the buildings, then walk along the walls for the harbour and the bay. Be ready for parked cars in the courtyard, which can spoil a wide shot. Step to one side, or frame tighter on a doorway, a wall or the church. For a view that takes in the fort walls and the yellow Governor's Palace together, try Gouvernementsplein as an alternative.
text.geographic_location: Fort Amsterdam is in the old centre of Willemstad, at the mouth of St. Anna Bay. It sits next to the harbour and the Governor's Palace.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Willemstad, at the mouth of St. Anna Bay, and look for the fort beside the harbour entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the fort itself, so once you are inside the walls you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard to fit in the walls and buildings, and the default lens (1x) for most other shots. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for details such as the church wall or the harbour from the ramparts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see the ochre walls and buildings of the fort. For the harbour and St. Anna Bay, walk along the walls to the ramparts.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the walls straight against the lines. If cars are parked in the courtyard, choose a tighter frame or shoot from a corner to keep them out. From the ramparts, put the water in the lower third and the sky above. For the fort walls and the Governor's Palace together, try Gouvernementsplein instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the yellow wall to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the ochre does not wash out in bright sun. Use panorama along the ramparts for the harbour, and hold the phone steady as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is warmer on the yellow buildings.

text.access_note: The courtyard and walls are open to visitors, but entry to the Fort Church or the government offices may be restricted or ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Queen Emma Bridge
label: Queen Emma Bridge
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/894738774: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Koningin Emmabrug' (163 m across).
notes: The floating pontoon bridge that swings open for ships, known as the Swinging Old Lady.

text.description: The Queen Emma Bridge is a floating pontoon bridge across St. Anna Bay, joining the Punda and Otrobanda sides of Willemstad. Locals call it the "Swinging Old Lady" because it swings open to let ships through. That movement is what makes it such a good subject: you can photograph a long, pedestrian-only walkway one minute and a wide gap of open water the next. The bridge was built in 1888, and has been renovated several times since, most recently in 2005–2006. The lighting arches date from 1955, put up for a royal visit by Queen Juliana and Prince Bernhard. Cars stopped using the bridge in 1974, so people on foot now have it to themselves. When it swings open, two free ferries carry pedestrians across, which gives you a second photo opportunity. Allow a few minutes to watch the bridge swing, since the process only takes a few minutes. Keep your phone ready with the camera app open, and look for the arches and the line of the waterfront buildings as natural frames.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses St. Anna Bay in the middle of Willemstad, linking the Punda quarter with the Otrobanda quarter on the opposite shore.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so start from Punda, one of the two quarters on either side of St. Anna Bay, or from Otrobanda on the other. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long, low bridge and the water in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the lighting arches or people crossing.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge along the lower or upper third, keeping the horizon level. Include the lighting arches to give the picture a sense of scale. If the bridge is swinging open, hold the same spot and take a before-and-after pair, or try a Live Photo to capture the movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. In dim evening light, let night mode do its work and keep your phone as still as you can, for example by resting your elbows on a rail or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. If you want to see the bridge swing open, ask locally or check the official site, as we cannot promise a time.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public, pedestrian-only crossing; when it swings open, free ferries carry pedestrians across, but check the official site before you go for any current changes.

text.description: Otrobanda is one of the historic quarters of Willemstad, on the south-west side of the city, facing Punda across Sint Anna Bay. Its name means 'the other side', and it was founded in 1707. Today it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for Willemstad, and it is a good place to wander with a phone in your hand. It works as a set of small scenes rather than one single view: old restored buildings, the waterfront at Brionplein, and the sea beside Rif Fort. Rif Fort has coral walls 1.5 metres thick, and the fort village is described as giving wide views over Punda and the water. The Curaçao Museum and the Kurá Hulanda Museum are also in the quarter, and the Queen Emma Bridge, nicknamed 'The Swinging Old Lady', links it to Punda. For photos, look for the contrast between old walls and bright details, and for the view back across the bay to Punda. Take a few wide shots of a street or square to show the setting, then move closer for doors, shutters and textures. Rif Fort is described as having restaurants, bars and live entertainment, so keep your phone ready there too.
text.geographic_location: Otrobanda lies on the south-west side of Willemstad, on the opposite shore of Sint Anna Bay from Punda. Brionplein is its waterfront centrepiece, and Rif Fort sits at the western end by the bay entrance.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is about 290 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most street and waterfront shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in squares and narrow streets, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as rooflines, shutters or the Punda skyline across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon and building edges level. Frame a colourful façade with some sky or street around it to show the setting. At the waterfront, include the bay and the Punda side behind it for a sense of place. Take a mix of wide scenes and close details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main building, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright sky and sea do not wash out. Use portrait mode if you photograph people, and check the lens is clean before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the buildings. Midday sun can be harsh and bleach out the colours.

text.access_note: The streets and waterfront are part of the quarter, but individual museums, the fort village and other sites may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kurá Hulanda Museum
label: Kurá Hulanda Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/295125529: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museum Kurá Hulanda'.
notes: Museum of the transatlantic slave trade in Otrobanda.

text.description:
The Kurá Hulanda Museum sits in Otrobanda, on the western side of Willemstad's harbour, in a cluster of restored old buildings. It teaches about the Atlantic slave trade and African history in the Caribbean, and it stands on the old quayside where slave ships once arrived, close to the site of the slave market. That history gives the place a quiet weight, and it is worth keeping in mind when you choose what to photograph and how.

The museum opened in April 1999, an initiative of the Dutch entrepreneur Jacob Gelt Dekker. He bought derelict buildings on the quay and market and restored them. Today the museum is spread across 15 buildings, so the area feels like a small village of courtyards and old walls rather than one single block.

For a phone photo, think of the setting rather than one big landmark. Look for the restored façades, doorways and the lines of the old buildings, which make good frames with a little sky above. Stand back far enough to get a whole façade in, then move in for a detail such as a doorway, a shutter or a texture in the wall. Keep the phone level using the gridlines so the vertical lines of the buildings stay straight. If you go inside, check the official site first for what is allowed, because photography rules in museums can differ from room to room. Be thoughtful about photographing other visitors and staff.
text.geographic_location: In the Kura Hulanda Village district of Willemstad, on the western quayside in Otrobanda. It stands by the old quayside, next to the Kurá Hulanda hotel buildings on the hillside.
text.directions_text: No tram or station stops are listed for this spot. Start from the Otrobanda area of Willemstad and walk towards the old western quayside, where the museum buildings stand. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the buildings as they look to the eye. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in narrow courtyards or lanes, where you cannot step back, but keep the phone upright so the walls do not lean. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for doorways, signs and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It is right at the museum. Look around for the façades and the buildings nearby, and choose the one you want to frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines. Frame a whole façade first, with some sky and a bit of the street for scale. Then take a closer shot of one detail, such as a doorway or a window. Wait a moment for people to move out of the frame if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Tap a shaded doorway if you want that detail to be clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Check the museum's own opening times on the official site.

text.access_note: This is a museum and ticketed access is likely, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light in Curaçao.
Museums often have different photography rules in different rooms, so inside photography may be restricted.
Entry to the museum is likely to be ticketed.
The area around the museum has narrow courtyards and lanes.

name: Rif Fort
label: Rif Fort
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

text.description:
Rif Fort is a 19th-century defensive fort at the mouth of Sint Anna Bay, on the Otrobanda side of Willemstad. It was built to guard the island, and its walls are made of coral stone about 1.5 metres thick. It once held more than 56 cannons. Today the old walls shelter Rif Fort Village, with restaurants, bars and shops, and the sea still breaks against the outer edges.

It photographs well because of the contrast between the heavy, pale walls and the open water and sky around them. Otrobanda itself dates from 1707 and is part of Willemstad's UNESCO-listed historic centre, so the surrounding streets and buildings make good context for a wider shot. The fort also looks across the bay towards Punda, which gives you a second subject on the same walk.

For your phone, think of this spot in two parts. Walk closer and you can fill the frame with the wall texture, arches and the sea along the fort's edge. Keep your horizon level using the gridlines, and take a few frames each time, because walkers, sea spray and bright sky can change a shot quickly.
text.geographic_location: Rif Fort is in the western part of Otrobanda, on the southwest side of Willemstad, at the entrance to Sint Anna Bay. Across the water lies the Punda side of the city.
text.directions_text: From there the fort is about 400 m to the north, roughly 6 minutes on foot. Head north towards the bay entrance and the fort will be ahead of you. The phone icon on the map is about 400 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fort in its surroundings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out wall details and the waves from a distance. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you get close and want to include the walls and the sky together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 400 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. It is roughly 6 minutes on foot from the fort, so use this point for the wider view and walk closer for detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep the horizon and the fort walls level. Place the fort on one third of the frame and leave the sea or sky on the other. If you move closer, look for the thick coral walls as a foreground and keep a little water or the Punda skyline behind them. Keep your phone steady against your body or a wall, as you will not have a tripod.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its texture. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the waves near the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stone than the middle of the day. Check the sun's direction on the day, as it will decide which side of the fort is lit.

text.access_note: Rif Fort now holds shops, restaurants and entertainment, so parts of it may have set opening times or rules; check the official site before you go.

notes: The famous row of pastel Dutch colonial buildings along the Punda waterfront.

text.description:
Handelskade is a waterfront street in Willemstad, and it can work well for phone photos if it gives you a line of buildings with water beside it. If the street has a row of colourful buildings, they make a good subject. Strong colours and repeating shapes make a picture easy to read, even on a small screen. If water is in the frame, calm conditions can give reflections.

The simplest approach is to treat the street as a long, flat band of colour. Stand back far enough to fit a good stretch of the row, then turn the phone to landscape. If you want a closer, more graphic shot, move in and photograph just two or three façades, keeping the vertical lines straight. Switch on the gridlines so the rooflines and any water's edge sit level.

If people or vehicles pass through, waiting a few seconds for a gap usually gives a cleaner frame, but a passer-by in a bright top can also add scale and life. Look for details as well as the wide view: shutters, doorways, shop signs and the way colours sit side by side.
text.geographic_location: Handelskade is a waterfront street in Willemstad.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, and no public transport stops are listed at all. The spot can be reached on foot from central Willemstad. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole street scene in one frame, but keep the main subject away from the edges of the picture, where buildings can look stretched. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a few façades and flatten the perspective.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take your first shots from here, then walk the couple of minutes towards the subject for closer frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone to landscape and switch on the gridlines. If water is in view, line its edge up with a horizontal grid line, and keep the buildings' vertical edges parallel to the vertical lines. Leave a little space around the subject for breathing room. For a second picture, zoom to 2x or more and fill the frame with two or three façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If the phone offers panorama mode, move slowly and keep the phone level for a long, clean sweep of the row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer colour on painted walls. Midday sun can be harsh and bleach the colours. Check the light on the day, as it depends on which way the façades face.

text.access_note: Handelskade is a street on the waterfront, so it should be open to walk along, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures.

name: Curaçao Synagogue
label: Mikvé Israel Synagogue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mikvé Israel-Emanuel Synagogue' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/312133712: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mikvé Israel-Emanuel' (47 m across).
notes: Oldest synagogue in continuous use in the Americas, with a sand floor.

text.description: The Curaçao Synagogue, known locally as the Snoa, is a calm yellow building in the Punda district of Willemstad. Its bright front, arched entrance and tall windows make it an easy subject for a phone, and the colour stands out well against a blue sky. The congregation, Mikvé Israel-Emanuel, was founded in 1651 and the building was completed in 1732. It is described as the oldest surviving synagogue in the Americas, and it is still in use today. Inside, the floor is covered in sand, and the interior is said to resemble the Portuguese Synagogue in Amsterdam. A Jewish historical museum is attached. The phone icon on the map sits on the building itself, so step out onto Hanchi di Snoa and shoot the facade from the street. From there the full front, with its arched entrance, fits well in a single frame. Punda is a busy part of town, so take a moment to frame the facade around parked cars and passers-by. Photography inside may be restricted, particularly during services, so check the signage on arrival. Most visitors will be happy with the exterior shot, and it costs nothing to take.
text.geographic_location: The synagogue is at Hanchi di Snoa 29 in Punda, in the city of Willemstad.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Punda district of Willemstad and look for Hanchi di Snoa. Once there, look for the yellow building. The phone icon on the map sits on the building itself, so step out onto the street and shoot the facade from there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the front. If the street is narrow and you cannot fit the whole facade in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the building centred so the edges do not lean or stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them so the walls stay straight. Include the arched entrance and enough sky to show the colour contrast. Wait for gaps in the traffic and pedestrians, or use them to add a little life to the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright and the wall looks washed out. Do not use flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light is softer and less harsh on the exterior.

text.access_note: The synagogue is an active place of worship and a visitor site with an attached museum, so entry and interior photography may be restricted; check the signage on arrival.

name: Queen Juliana Bridge
label: Queen Juliana Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Handelskade' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Handelskade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/919681206: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Koningin Julianabrug' (511 m across).
notes: One of the highest bridges in the Caribbean, spanning the harbour entrance.

text.description:
Queen Juliana Bridge is the big arch that carries traffic over St. Anna Bay in Willemstad, linking the Punda and Otrobanda sides of the city. It is a four-lane road bridge, and at its highest point it stands 56.4 metres above the water, so that ships can pass into the narrow harbour. It opened on 30 April 1974 and is named after Juliana of the Netherlands. Once it was finished, the older Queen Emma Bridge was closed to traffic and now carries only pedestrians.

The bridge photographs well because it sits behind one of the most colourful scenes in town. From Handelskade on the Punda waterfront, the arch rises over the bay behind the painted buildings, with the harbour water in the foreground. That gives you sky, curve, colour and water in one frame, which suits a phone screen nicely.

The bridge is for vehicles only and has no pedestrian walkway, so you can't walk up to the top for a photo. It is hard to photograph from a moving car, so it is better to enjoy the bridge from the waterfront. If you have time, De Rouvilleweg in Otrobanda and Rif Fort offer different angles, described below. Take your time on Handelskade, keep an eye on passing traffic, and take a few frames at different zoom levels before you move on.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses St. Anna Bay in central Willemstad, joining the Punda and Otrobanda districts. Handelskade, the Punda waterfront street, is the recommended nearby viewpoint.
text.directions_text: Head for Handelskade on the Punda waterfront. Handelskade is the place to stand, with the pair of antique cannons as a landmark. From there the bridge lies to the north, across the bay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the waterfront buildings and the whole arch together. Then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier, more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pick out the arch above the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Handelskade (Punda waterfront, near the pair of antique cannons). The bridge rises across St. Anna Bay behind the colourful waterfront buildings of Punda, with the harbour in the foreground. This is the classic ground-level view of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the lower line, so the bridge sits across the upper part of the frame. Use the coloured buildings and the water as the lower part of the picture rather than cutting them off. For a different angle, Rif Fort gives a higher, angled view of the arch with Punda spread out below, and De Rouvilleweg in Otrobanda frames the bridge in the distance on a quieter residential street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Check that the arch is straight against the gridlines before you take the shot. A short burst or a Live Photo can help if boats or people cross the frame.

name: Scharloo
label: Scharloo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bargestraat' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bargestraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9507098: large area 'Scharloo' (1595 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic merchants' quarter with restored colourful mansions.

text.description: Scharloo is the neighbourhood of Willemstad where old merchant wealth turned into colour. It began in 1634 as a Dutch West Indies Company plantation, but the soil was poor and the plantation was soon abandoned. From 1870 wealthy Jewish merchants built villas here, and after the 1877 hurricane the area grew quickly into the richest part of the city. It declined in the 1960s, was renovated in the early 21st century, and has been part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre since 1999. For photos, the best street is Bargestraat, where a row of brightly painted colonial houses stands beside wall murals. Several photo guides single it out for exactly that mix. The houses give you strong colour and neat repeating shapes, and the murals add a human touch. If you have time, Scharlooweg is the main street, with the largest villas. Its best-known building is Bolo di Batrei (the Wedding Cake) at number 77, which now houses the National Archive of Curaçao. The Dare building carries the Three O'Clock Romance mural by Francis Sling, with two birds painted across its front. Murals can be repainted or covered, so treat what you see on arrival as the current version. Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the facades, and frame from the public pavement.
text.geographic_location: Scharloo is a historic neighbourhood of Willemstad. A bridge built in 1881 connected it with Pietermaai. Bargestraat is one of its streets.
text.directions_text: From there, Scharloo lies about 350 m to the east, a short walk of around 4 to 5 minutes. Scharlooweg and the Dare building are other photo options in Scharloo; check their exact positions on arrival. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole street of painted houses and murals. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a single facade or mural with less distortion. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as balconies, gables or the two birds on the Dare building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bargestraat. A row of brightly painted colonial houses with wall murals along the street. Stay on the public pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the line of house fronts parallel to the grid so the street looks tidy. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full row, then step in for a close shot of one mural with a doorway or balcony beside it. For a different view, try Scharlooweg, with the restored mansions' gables, balconies and entrances in the frame. Or step back from the Dare building to fit its whole facade and both birds into one picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Keep the phone level to stop the tall facades leaning inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is gentler and the colours look warmer.

text.access_note: Bargestraat and Scharlooweg are public streets, but many of the buildings are offices, government agencies or museums, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Waterfort
label: Waterfort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rif Fort' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rif Fort' (node/295125530): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/312133432: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Water Fort' (358 m across).
notes: Old fortification along the shore, now an arcade of shops and restaurants.

text.description:
The Waterfort is a nineteenth-century fort on the eastern side of Sint Anna Bay, at the Punda end of the harbour channel in Willemstad. It was built from 1827 to guard the town, and it went with a twin fort, Rif Fort, planned for the opposite bank. Marines were stationed here from 1858, and in 1955 the Plaza Hotel Curaçao was built inside the walls. That mix of old fortification and working hotel is what you see today. The photo here is the long, heavy outer wall rising from the water, with the Punda waterfront beside it.

The best frame is the classic counter-view from the ramparts of Rif Fort, on the other side of the channel. From there you look across the harbour mouth to the Waterfort and the Punda waterfront, with water in the foreground to give the picture depth. Because the hotel occupies the inside of the fort, photograph it from the outside, from the walls or the quay, rather than going in. Rif Fort has shops and restaurants, but its walls can be climbed and the area is open to the public. If you would like a second angle, the Koningin Emmabrug has the Punda waterfront and the channel, with the Waterfort near the Punda end of the bridge, though there it plays a supporting part. Wall and quay access can be restricted at times, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Willemstad, on the Punda (eastern) side of the Sint Anna Bay channel, where the harbour opens to the sea. The Waterfort is across the channel from Rif Fort, on the western side of the harbour.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so make your way to Rif Fort, on the western side of the channel. Walk up onto the ramparts and stop. From there the Waterfort lies to the south-east, across the water, so you photograph it from the opposite bank rather than walking to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fort wall and the waterfront together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the water and sky, and 2x-3x telephoto to pick out the fort wall and the waterfront buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Rif Fort (ramparts on the western side of the channel, looking east across the harbour mouth to Punda). The Waterfort and the Punda waterfront across the channel, framed from the fort walls of Rif Fort. Stay on the open walls rather than going into the shops or restaurants.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fort wall along the lower third, with the water beneath it and the sky above. Keep the horizon level. Include a bit of the rampart edge in the foreground if you want to show you are looking across from another fort. For a different angle, the Koningin Emmabrug gives a view of the Punda waterfront and channel with the Waterfort near the Punda end of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the stonework and colours do not wash out. A Live Photo can catch boats moving through the channel.

text.access_note: Rif Fort's walls can be climbed and the area is open to the public, but the Waterfort itself is partly a hotel and wall and quay access may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Rif Fort ramparts, the Waterfort lies to the south-east, so a late-afternoon or sunset sun behind you should light the fort wall.
Water in the foreground and a level horizon along the gridlines give a balanced composition.
Boats pass through the channel often enough for a Live Photo to catch one.
The Koningin Emmabrug view includes the Waterfort near the Punda end of the bridge as a secondary element.

name: Sint Anna Bay
label: Sint Anna Bay
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9510882: large area 'Sint Annabaai' (1584 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The channel that splits Willemstad into Punda and Otrobanda.

text.description:
Sint Anna Bay is the deep channel that splits Willemstad in two, with Punda on one bank and Otrobanda on the other. It is about a mile long and up to 1,000 feet wide. At the southern end it opens into the Caribbean Sea. At the northern end it leads into the Schottegat, the big inner lagoon and industrial area. It separates the two parts of Willemstad, Punda and Otrobanda.

It photographs well because the water gives you a clear, open foreground, with a long line of waterfront buildings on either side. On a phone, the bay works best as a wide, simple scene: the water, the two banks and a lot of sky. Because the channel is long and fairly narrow, you can also use it to lead the eye along the picture towards the far end.

Take a few frames along the way as the view opens up. Keep your phone steady against your body or a railing, and wipe the lens first, as sea air leaves a film on it. If ships or boats are passing, wait for one to enter the frame, because it gives the scene a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Sint Anna Bay is the channel running between Punda and Otrobanda, the two halves of central Willemstad. It connects the Caribbean Sea in the south with the Schottegat lagoon to the north.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so head to the Punda/Otrobanda waterfront in central Willemstad. The bay lies about 202 m to the north-east of it, about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the channel, both banks and plenty of sky into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat or a section of the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk a little closer if you want the channel to fill more of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon on a lower or upper line so it sits level. Let the edge of the water lead the eye towards the far end of the channel. Leave some sky in the shot. Try one wide shot with the ultra-wide (0.5x) and one tighter shot at 2x or more of a boat or building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water or the buildings to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the sky down slightly so it keeps its colour. If a boat is moving, a short Live Photo can give you a choice of frames afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and more comfortable temperatures. Around midday the sun is high and the water can look flat and glary.

text.access_note: The bay is a stretch of open water seen from the waterfront, but access to individual quays or piers may vary, so check locally before you go.

name: Basilica of St. Anne
label: Basilica St. Anne
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 24 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 380 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/370349178: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sint Anna Basiliek' (61 m across).

text.description:
The Basilica of St. Anne is a small Catholic church in Willemstad, built between 1734 and 1752. It became a Minor Basilica in 1975, when Pope Paul VI granted it the status, and it also serves as a co-cathedral of the Diocese of Willemstad. It is counted among the world's smallest basilica churches, so you are photographing a modest building rather than a grand one. It is part of the Historic Area of the city and port of Willemstad, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.

That makes it a distant view rather than a close-up. Use this spot for the church in its setting, and give yourself time to look for a clear gap between buildings, trees and passing traffic. If you want the doorway or the façade in detail, walk the short distance towards the church and take a second set of photos there.

Keep your phone level, switch on the gridlines so the walls stay upright, and take a few frames at different zoom levels. Small differences in position can change what sits in front of the church, so move a step or two sideways if something is in the way. Do not go inside just to take pictures. It is a working church, so check the official site before you go if you plan to visit.
text.geographic_location: The basilica is in the Otrabanda sector of Willemstad. It lies within the Historic Area of the city and port of Willemstad.
text.directions_text: It is a short walk in that compass direction, so keep the church tower and roofline in view as you approach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the basilica closer from where you stand. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider view with the surroundings. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for close-up shots near the church, where it helps you fit in the whole façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Queen Emma Bridge (Otrobanda end, looking back across the bay). The Otrobanda side of St. Anna Bay from the pontoon bridge, with the basilica about 270 m northwest of the bridge, so it may be visible only as a distant element. Face that direction and look for a clear line of sight to the church. Take one wide shot at 1x first, then zoom in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the church near one third of the frame, with the sky or street space around it for context. Line the vertical edges of the walls up with the grid lines so the building does not lean. Tap the church to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the church and adjust the exposure slider so the walls keep their detail. When zoomed in, hold the phone with both hands and rest your elbows against your body to keep it steady. Take two or three frames of each view and pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Check how the light falls on the façade when you arrive.

text.access_note: The basilica is a place of worship and part of a UNESCO-listed area, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

text.description:
The Floating Market is a market in Willemstad, and the name suggests what to look for: you may see stalls and boats at the water's edge, with produce for sale and people chatting. It is likely to be a lively, busy scene, which makes it a good place for candid, everyday photos rather than posed ones. Reflections in the water, bright colours and the mix of boats and buildings can give you plenty to work with, even on a short visit.

The market itself is the subject, so use that distance for one wide establishing shot, then walk closer for details. Start with the default lens (1x) and keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the row of boats and stalls is too long to fit. Then use 2x or 3x for close shots of produce, hands and faces, which is also kinder to people who may not want a phone right in front of them. Ask before photographing anyone closely.

What is open and where the boats tie up can change from day to day, so treat this as a flexible stop. Look for a clear patch of quayside, tap on the brightest colour to focus, and pull the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the scene.
text.directions_text: Walk east and you will reach the market. The phone icon on the map is about 250 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the line of boats and stalls will not fit, and 2x or 3x telephoto for close-ups of produce and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 250 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Then walk east, about 3 to 4 minutes on foot, to the quayside for closer shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the water's edge level. Put the stalls on one third of the frame and the water and reflections on the rest. Hold the ultra-wide lens back from the edge, as it stretches anything near the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest awning or fruit to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich. Try a Live Photo for the movement of people and boats, then choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is usually the liveliest time for a market, and the light is softer then. Avoid the harsh midday sun if you can.

text.access_note: Trading days, hours and any access rules are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Floating Market may have stalls and boats at the water's edge with produce for sale (inferred from the name only).
Markets like this are usually busiest and best in the morning, and the light is softer then.
Some stallholders and shoppers may not want to be photographed close up, so it is polite to ask first.
Which boats and stalls are present can vary from day to day.
